presentingComplaint: 2 days of high-grade fever with shaking chills, right-sided pleuritic chest pain, and a productive cough with rusty-tinged sputum.
history: Previously well 42-year-old man with no significant past medical history presents with abrupt onset of fever and rigors 2 days ago, followed by a productive cough with rust-colored sputum and right-sided pleuritic chest pain worse on deep inspiration. No preceding coryza or sore throat. No vomiting, diarrhea, or urinary symptoms. No recent hospitalization, antibiotic use, or travel. No smoking history. No known TB contact. Denies hemoptysis, weight loss, or night sweats. No immunocompromising conditions.
examination: Alert, oriented, appears unwell but not toxic. Flushed with dry lips (mild dehydration). Right lower zone shows dullness to percussion, increased tactile fremitus, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse crepitations. No wheeze. No cyanosis. No signs of meningism. No peripheral stigmata of endocarditis. Abdomen soft, non-tender.
imaging: Chest X-ray: dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, no effusion, no cavitation
microbiology: Sputum Gram stain: gram-positive diplococci, moderate polymorphs
Blood cultures x2 sent before antibiotics
finalDiagnosis: Community-acquired pneumonia (typical lobar pattern, likely pneumococcal), CURB-65 = 0-1, low severity, outpatient/short-stay candidate
citations: IDSA/ATS Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Adults Guideline 2019
stewardship: Empirical therapy for low-severity CAP in a previously healthy outpatient without comorbidities per IDSA/ATS 2019: amoxicillin as preferred monotherapy, or a macrolide (azithromycin) / doxycycline as alternative if local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is low; combination beta-lactam plus macrolide reserved for comorbidities or more severe disease. Narrow to targeted therapy once sputum/blood culture and urinary antigen results return. De-escalate and convert to oral therapy once clinically stable.
contraindications: Avoid fluoroquinolone monotherapy as first-line in low-severity CAP given resistance/adverse-effect concerns unless beta-lactam/macrolide contraindicated
Avoid delaying antibiotics pending culture results in a symptomatic febrile patient with radiographic consolidation
Caution with macrolides if QT-prolonging comorbidity or interacting drugs present (not applicable here but standard check)
edgeCases: If CURB-65 rises to >=2 or hypoxia worsens, escalate to inpatient combination therapy and reassess severity criteria
If patient fails to improve within 48-72h, consider resistant organism, empyema, or alternative diagnosis (e.g., PE) and repeat imaging
This case represents low-severity, previously well host; if immunocompromised or nursing-home resident, aspiration/HAP pathways would instead apply
expectedMaiK: MaiK should recognize a classic typical lobar CAP presentation (acute fever, rigors, productive/rusty sputum, pleuritic pain, focal consolidation) in a previously well adult, calculate a low CURB-65, and recommend outpatient-appropriate empirical therapy (amoxicillin or macrolide/doxycycline) rather than broad-spectrum escalation.
